Q&A: Ray Tintori Beasts of the Southern Wild

Q&A: Ray Tintori Beasts of the Southern Wild BY JANINE POURROY -s he approached his first full-length feature, Beasts of the Southern Wild, director Benh Zeitlin was determined to make the most out of assets he had used before: community and connectedness. These were the very qualities that had drawn him to his adopted home, New Orleans, and they were among the key themes driving the screenplay he had written with his longtime friend, Lucy Alibar, upon whose one-act play the story was based. They had also shaped a working model that Zeitlin and his band of best friends had embraced since their college days, and their production company, Court 13 — so named after the Wesleyan University squash court where many a student movie had been made - had a certain 'musical chairs' quality when it came to job descriptions. Shorts and music videos represented their entire body of work prior to the feature-length Beasts, but they had always worked together. Community and connectedness. This time, however, Zeitlin's collaborative vision was on a much grander scale. For Beasts of the Southern Wild, he persuaded Court 13 - along with a hundred friends and 1 / 15 family members - to assemble on the edge of a Southern Louisiana bayou, where he

RAY TINTORI intended to realize his most ambitious film project to date. Zeitlin and Alibar had crafted a story as elemental as life and death, but their setting was simply called the Bathtub, an isolated island settlement slowly eroding into the Gulf of Mexico. There, six-year-old Hushpuppy finds her place within her colorful and resilient community - and learns the rules of survival as she and her father, Wink, recover from the effects of a devastating storm. Hushpuppy must also come to terms with Wink's impending death, and she does so, in part, by facing her fear of the aurochs - a fierce and now-extinct beast she learns about as a cautionary tale in school. Called Nazie for short, Quvenzhane Wallis was just five years old when she auditioned for the pivotal role of Hushpuppy, and only six during the course of production. But with her expressive face and old-soul essence, this first-time actress immediately became the heartbeat of the film. The part of Wink was awarded to another newcomer, Dwight Henry, a local baker whose natural charm won over the filmmakers during their daily visits to his New Orleans bakery, located across the street from their casting office. Zeitlin was joined in his efforts by producers Josh Penn, Dan Janvey and Michael Gottwald, and by another old friend, Ray Tintori, who was given an original and curiously specific job title for his work on the movie: aurochs and special effects unit director. With an ambitious effects breakdown and a budget initially set at only $25,000, Tintori knew that resourcefulness would be the order of the day - and it remained so even when his effects allotment grew to a somewhat more reasonable $100,000. To deliver the film's effects, Tintori turned to pre-digital techniques: miniature sets, cloud 2 / 15 tank clouds, and - most audaciously - the use of real-life baby pigs as stand-ins for the

RAY TINTORI giant, prehistoric aurochs. The film's entire budget was a modest $1.5 million; and yet, Beasts of the Southern Wild went on to earn more than $11 million at the boxoffice in the months that followed its June 2012 premiere. The Fox Searchlight release also took home prizes from both Cannes and Sundance, fueling industry speculation that Academy Award nominations might soon be in the offing. Beasts of the Southern Wild is a special little film of the kind that tends to draw a small, but loyal following. In this case, it's managed to capture a large audience that now reaches around the world. It really is a small movie, and we knew there was a very good chance it wouldn't even make a sound, so we were as surprised as anyone by all the attention. It was the first project we did on this level with no grownups around. It was made with no studio notes at all. Zeitlin had final cut; he had actor approval; he made it exactly the way he wanted to. And we worked in a very utopian kind of way - it was like a bunch of kids getting together to make a movie. For it to get any kind of mainstream exposure at all is pretty amazing. There's been a lot of talk about the magical realism of the film, and Benh Zeitlin has said, 'The further you get from Louisiana, the movie plays more like a fantasy or a fairytale' - which implies that the closer you get to Louisiana, the more it plays like reality. Was that balance between fantasy and reality something you factored 3 / 15 into the effects?

RAY TINTORI When I first read the script, there was definitely some material that came across as 'high concept,' but the more time I spent in Louisiana, the more I came to recognize that it was real. For example, there are shots in the film that might seem like effects shots, but which were based on real occurrences. One is featured in the trailer, where Hushpuppy is standing in front of the water and it suddenly jumps. It looks like we used subwoofers or some other giant mechanism, but it came from something the crew just noticed: there were all these bugs on the surface of the water, and if you made a loud noise, they reacted all at once. It was just part of this teeming ecosystem down there. When he was traveling around doing location scouting, Zeitlin would see things that were surreal looking and think, 'I've got to figure out a way to write that into the film.' Is that also true about places like the Bathtub? The Bathtub is Zeitlin's idealized version of those communities, but it definitely comes from examining the people who live there and getting to know them. When Zeitlin started exploring the region, he was adopted by a variety of families that wanted to show him everything. They were rabidly genuine and generous people - and they left you feeling a little ashamed to be from the city. Many American movies make the point that everywhere in America is exactly the same: strip mall, strip mall, strip mall. Everyone watches the same TV shows; everyone's stuck with the same problems. When people see our film they realize, 'Oh, there are parts of America that are real and exist right now that I had no idea about.' Zeitlin has described the story, in part, as 'a series of mythological and environ4 / 15 mental catastrophes' that Hushpuppy has to learn how to survive. By remarkable

RAY TINTORI coincidence, your first day of filming was the same day as the 2010 BP Deepwater Horizon explosion in the Gulf of Mexico. How did that real-life cataclysm shape the course of production? It was like the Army descended. The marina right down the road from our office and the main sets became the launching point for the cleanup. BP started taking over, and we had to negotiate with them to be able to shoot there. One of the key effects shots shows the aurochs swimming through the water, and as we were shooting that scene with large-scale puppets, the guys with the foam booms - those big floatation devices they use to contain surface oil - kept screaming past us as we were filming. It felt like we were doing a puppet show in the middle of a war zone. An aurochs is a real, extinct animal, but it's also a beautiful metaphor for both the natural world and the people of the Bathtub. Were you conscious of this as you developed the effects? The aurochs were supposed to function pretty much the way guitar solos do. Beasts has a lot of things in common with indie films that people know they should watch, but where it kind of feels like eating your vegetables. It was clear to us that adding this fantastical element might help, if used rightly. It gave the film a dose of spectacle, which is partly why people go to the movies in the first place. If the aurochs turned out to be underwhelming, they were going to have to be cut. You had only worked on music videos and shorts prior to Beasts. How did that prepare you to take on the role of special effects supervisor for this film? 5 / 15 I had made a music video for a band called MGMT that used animatronics and a

RAY TINTORI bunch of '80s-type scary monsters - and which featured an eighteen-month-old baby. We pulled out all of the Cinefex magazines that gave me nightmares when I was five, and tried to make creatures like the ones in those old articles. Based on my experience with animatronics and nonverbal beings, I became the de facto effects expert. Those past scary monsters would typically be done as puppets or animatronics; and today, of course, they would be done as CO characters. Did you consider using any of those techniques? We did use simple puppets in some cases. But we knew that even if we worked really hard on an animatronic, the aurochs wouldn't come close to being a Dark Crystal-quality creature, for example. We also knew that we didn't have enough money to do it right in CG. So, we came up with this Hail Mary pass of dressing up baby pigs and putting them into miniature sets. That was a bold idea. Actually, it was a really bad idea. We looked hard for some kind of reference material, to give us confidence that it could work - 'God, someone else must have dressed up an animal before!' But we could only find one shot from Stargate where they costumed a dog and had it pulling a James Spader Ken doll through the desert for, maybe, two seconds. Nobody had done this - because you wouldn't do this if you had any other choice. In our case, however, it was a matter of having a script that was unfilmable for our budget. We had to use live animals, and then figure out how to do so without it being a travesty. What made you decide on baby pigs, of all things? 6 / 15 Based on our research, it was either dogs or pigs. We needed an animal that was

RAY TINTORI trainable. Also, pigs, especially when they're young, have body proportions that are kind of strange. If you don't show their feet, it's hard to determine exactly what they are. We went out to a farm and shot some test footage in slow motion with this one little baby pig, just to see how it might work, and we discovered that if we shot the pig at the correct angles and really close, there was a certain spectacle to it. It was mesmerizing. Another thing we learned as we went along was that pigs have a very dainty, prissy kind of walk, and that gives away their scale. But if they're running at full speed they take on a horselike gait, which looks really good in slow motion. How did you approach the training process? You have to start training a pig at the earliest possible age, and then raise it to be unlike any other pig - a pig that is comfortable around people. We got our main actor pig, Oliver, when he was just a week and a half old. Our trainer, Kate Bryant - her official job title was animal tamer - has a very methodical and precise mind, and she spent months conditioning Oliver and four other baby pigs to get them to perform. We were shooting on 16mm film in slow motion, and the amount of light we had to use was really intense. Also, we were always testing prototype costumes on them - and getting a baby animal to wear a fur coat and prosthetic horns coming off its head while standing on a table under Klieg lights surrounded by people, was hard. We learned right away that they didn't like standing on tables, for example - they'd just hop off the back and run into the corner of the room. It became clear early on that everything hinged on whether or not the animals were comfortable with the techniques we were using. We had to train 7 / 15 the pigs to understand that they were safe so they wouldn't revolt at the situation.

RAY TINTORI I understand that you shot the pigs over a period of nine days, after principal photography had wrapped. How did you manage to get everything you needed in only nine days? They were good, well-trained pigs, for one thing. Another part of it was seeing what we could get them to do, and then building sequences around that. We learned this by watching a lot of David Attenborough nature documentaries. We realized that although the stories were cut together like a narrative, the filmmakers were actually building narratives around actions the animals would do over and over again. With the pigs, all of our sequences were like setups. We figured out that if we needed the pigs to do this kind of action, we were going to be able to cover it in these kinds of ways - which we could then cut together into a sequence. We definitely had actions we were looking for, but we would set things in motion and wait until we caught them. The pigs also learned to do certain tricks. For example, you can get a pig to turn around on command, and then if you cut in at the end of it, you can make it look like it's turning around to see something. They could lock eyes on things; they could hit a mark. They could even kneel. That scene at the end of the movie, for instance, where the aurochs bows down before Hushpuppy, was originally written as 'the aurochs backs away.' But it became a script piece when we discovered that pigs can kneel down on their front haunches. How 'direct-able' is a pig, even a well-trained one? Not very. Basically, you have to change everything around them in order to get the 8 / 15 performance you want. For instance, there's a point in the aurochs' journey where they're

RAY TINTORI tired and struggling to go forward. Unfortunately, you can't get a pig to respond correctly when you say, 'I need you to pretend you're having difficulty with this now,' so we had to figure out a way to get around it. To slow them down, we built a system of 30-degree ramps. We would lead them up to the starting gate, and then have them climb up these ramps to get to the set. We built the set itself at a 45-degree angle, and dressed it with dirt and mud brought up from the bayou - just smeared it with our hands on a carpeted surface. We then hung a big painted backdrop behind it and shot it at the same 45-degree angle. Even though the pigs were actually climbing up this hill, it looked like they were on level ground - and it worked great. How did you arrive at costuming them in little fur coats? The credit for that goes to Matt Thompson, Court 13's resident engineer, the guy we go to every time we need to invent something new. He went through about 30 different designs, and tried every kind of synthetic fur and fabric he could find, but nothing really worked. Finally someone said, 'How about we use nutria?' Nutria are a kind of swamp rat that's specific to the region - but they're pests, and people get paid to kill them, so there are furs everywhere. We dyed some nutria fur black, and it turned out to be exactly the right thing. And it seemed right that the costumes for the miniature aurochs came from something that was indigenous to that area. Throughout the rest of the film - for all the live-action sets - they used pieces of things they found locally and kind of cobbled them together. Even the big aurochs puppets were dressed with the inside of palm tree bark that we just picked up off the ground. Everything we did was basically stitched 9 / 15 together from swamp rats and stolen pieces.

RAY TINTORI You had the aurochs moving through several landscapes throughout the film. How did you create a range of different settings with such limited time and resources? We built one basic set made up of tables that were about two feet wide; and when we put them all together, they created a 32-foot-long track that was fairly low to the ground. We used that same track for everything. We put sand on it, and it was a desert; we put little cardboard buildings on it, and it was a favela. We also had a really good art department. The crews came in off the shoot in the bayou and went straight to work on our miniatures, painting backgrounds on canvas on a 10-by-60-foot frame. They'd set up the frame, paint it, and then, at the end of the day, take it down and start painting the next one. They were really fast. It sounds like you had a very resourceful crew. How many people were you working with? The unit I had was pretty small - between five and eight people. While everyone else was down in the bayou shooting the live-action, we were in New Orleans, in a neighborhood called the Marigny. We took over an abandoned 1916 firehouse and turned it into our effects shop. The initial plan was to shoot there, but at a certain point it became clear that it was going to be a nightmare. Luckily, we found a funky old soundstage called 9th Ward Studios where they shot parts of Easy Rider. It had a lot more space, and it was better for the bright lights we needed for the miniature work. Of course, the lighting also made the set very hot. Pigs can't control their body temperature very well; so, to keep them comfortable, we got a massive industrial air conditioner and blasted them 10 / 15 with cool air - and had them stand in little kiddie pools between takes.

RAY TINTORI The soundstage also provided a certain level of control over the shoot. The rest of the movie was so freewheeling - 'We're not going to build a set with flyaway walls, we're going to follow Nazie around instead!' - but you can't just follow a pig around with a camera. We had enough chaos built in from the beginning, just by shooting pigs. We couldn't spend our entire budget endlessly shooting garbage footage. in one sequence, the aurochs stampede through a favela and demolish it. How did you do that? The shot originally called for adobe huts, but we thought the favela would work better because it had sharper angles - and the buildings were similar to the structures that the people of the Bathtub lived in. We couldn't spend the time it would take to make them beautiful because we knew we were going to trash them, so we built a lot of modular, easily-replicated miniature pieces from cardboard. Then, Matt Thompson's brother, Alex, laser-cut beautiful little bicycles and gates and antennas out of very thin cardboard. So we had all these cruddy, easily breakable pieces mixed in with elegant little laser-cut pieces - and we had the pigs running and smashing through it all. To shoot it, our DP, Ben Richardson, wore an Easyrig and sat on a dolly low to the ground. We pushed the dolly as fast as possible to keep up with the pigs as they ran, and we got some pretty wild, spontaneous action as a result. Of course, there was no way to get closeups on a pig with that setup, no way we could pull focus on, say, the tip of a horn or part of a hoof. So in addition to the dolly shots, we shot inserts with the pig on a treadmill - which meant he was more or less in 1 / 15 one place and we could shoot those details. Our lead artist, Sam Wohl, designed and

RAY TINTORI operated a treadmill powered by a bicycle, which gave us really good control over speeding up and slowing down. Every day we'd train the pig to go a little bit faster, and by the end it was galloping at full speed on that treadmill. This might be a good time to ask: no pigs were harmed in the making of this film, right? We didn't hurt any of the pigs, ever - but it was pretty chaotic. For the favela sequence, we used a sock puppet pig for some of the more aggressive action. We sculpted a latex pig head, put a costume on it, and plowed that through one of our models. One of the first times we see the aurochs is when it's frozen in ice, and then later, when it begins to break out of the ice. As you were doing the effects breakdown and conceptualizing those shots, what movie references were most helpful to you? Zeitlin wanted all of the effects in Beasts to remind you of films from the '80s - films you'd seen as a little kid, but that were really too scary for you to watch. As reference, we thought about movies like Neverending Story, Willow and Ghostbusters. For the aurochs breaking out of the ice, specifically, we recalled the scene in Ghostbusters where the helldogs break out of the statues. We all had vivid memories of that sequence - or thought we did. When we went back and actually looked at it, it was completely different than what we remembered. Very little was actually revealed. We had mentally filled in the helldogs sequence with what was not there. We decided to do the same thing with the aurochs breaking out of the ice, showing it in a series of very quick shots. In the end, there are actually very few shots of the aurochs in the entire movie. They're mostly 12 / 15 hinted at. It isn't until the end of the film, when Hushpuppy comes face-to-face with it

RAY TINTORI on the bridge, that you actually get a good look at the aurochs. And that's when you can see its kindness and wisdom. That 'they can see each other' moment works because we don't show the aurochs clearly earlier. You did that moment as a greenscreen composite? Yes. We spent two days shooting the pigs in front of a greenscreen with a RED digital camera, which was a very precise and methodical process. They'd already shot all the live-action stuff, so it was just a matter of gathering as much basic information with the pigs as we could - and shooting it as high-res as possible. And Ben Richardson was adamant about filming the live-action portions exactly as they had filmed the rest of the movie on location, with the actors moving around very naturally and the camera following them documentary style. Of course, that made the compositing incredibly difficult - not just for this shot, but for all the shots in the film - and the effects houses I approached about it basically responded, 'We just don't want to do that much work.' Who ultimately did those difficult composites? Brendan Bellomo and Catherine Tate were the visual effects supervisors. Brendan was passionate about it. He's really an artist, and he was definitely not in it for the money. Things like compositing Nazie's hair were a nightmare, but it was really important to Zeitlin that we keep it authentic. Brendan just killed himself on the compositing, often adding elements that he created himself. For instance, for the sequence where the aurochs crash through the favela, Brendan went out to the parking lot and shot shovelfuls of dirt that he threw up in the air, and then layered those elements into the shot to create 13 / 15 flying dust and debris.

RAY TINTORI Not all of the effects in the movie involve the aurochs. There's a sequence, for example, in which a levee explodes. How did you shoot that? Alex Thompson made a really nice quarter-scale model based on the real levee where they shot the live-action, using concoctions of foamy concrete that broke apart easily in miniature. For the explosion itself, we had to try out the miniature explosives to get the shape we wanted. I wasn't sure we had it right, so I asked one of the explosive guys to do it again. He looked at me like he was about to cry, and said: 'Do you understand that each of these tests costs 12 dollars? I can't keep doing tests. There's not enough money!' Given that the budget was always a concern, were there other old-school effects techniques, in addition to miniatures, that you resurrected for this film? Again, we scoured old Cinefex magazines to figure out how to make clouds, which we mostly used in the Antarctic sequence, when the camera starts on the aurochs in ice and pans up to the sky. As we read, we kept coming across this one name: Gary Platek. Gary did cloud tank effects for Poltergeist, Ghostbusters and a number of other films; but in the Ghostbusters issue of Cinefex, we saw exactly what we wanted our clouds to look like. So, Rob Leitzell, who designed our forced-perspective sets, engineered and built a 300-gallon, four-by-four-foot cloud tank for us, and then we employed some of the techniques Gary had used in Ghostbusters - things like using a T-shaped probe to create roiling clouds, and using a circular ring probe for the outside clouds. Even with the information in the Cinefex article, though, there were still certain 14 / 15 things we couldn't figure out; and so, I found Gary on Facebook and wrote him a long

RAY TINTORI email explaining what we'd already done, and what we were still struggling with. He wrote back, and said: 'I'm replying because you've done your homework. I get many requests for information, but most people don't even try it on their own.' And then he gave me the details of exactly how to do it. Now that you're able to look back at the project with 20/20 hindsight, what would you say was most satisfying for you? The most gratifying thing was that the aurochs were not a complete burden on the film. My main feeling going to work every day was, 'We cannot ruin Zeitlin's movie.' And then, when I actually saw the movie, there was a moment when I thought: 'Oh, my God, the aurochs are about to come on - is this when this sincere, intense live-action film is going to jump the shark?' That would have been terrible - because the movie was going great without them. The fact that the aurochs didn't sink the movie was the best I could ask for. The truth is, this movie wasn't about the aurochs or other big effects. It was about Hushpuppy, and Nazie's performance was really the antimatter that held it all together. The script had descriptions of some bells and whistles, and some of them worked and some of them didn't. But, in the end, the film was mostly closeups of Nazie's face. Their latest feature, Cloud Atlas, a challenging narrative that both demands and rewards an attentive audience, cements their reputation as cinematic risk-takers. Based on the award-winning bestseller by David Mitchell, the film explores how the actions of individuals influence one another in the past, present and future. In his novel, Mitchell told six stories with a palindromic set of chapters nested in time. The Wachowskis and co-writer/director Tom Tykwer tell the same stories, but intercut them through the narrative, moving back and forth in time and place. iThe film is incredibly faithful to the book in spirit, but not literally, said Dan Glass, production visual effects supervisor and executive vice president at Method Studios. '¿The book implies that actions in one time affect another, but the film explicitly portrays that idea, playing on causes and consequences across time." Each story takes place in a different year - 1849, 1931, 1974, 2012, 2144, 2321 - 1 / 27 and features actors playing not only multiple roles, but also different genders and races.

The Calculus of Pi BY JODY DUNCAN n 2002, novelist Yann Martel won the distinguished Man Booker Prize for fiction for his moving and metaphorical Life of Pi, an inspirational story in which a middle-aged Pi Patel recalls for a writer the life-changing events of his youth. Leaving his native India aboard a freighter bound for Canada, with his family and many of the animals from their zoo in Pondicherry, Pi becomes the sole human survivor when the ship sinks in a storm. He then endures an eight-month ordeal at sea as he struggles to survive the perils of the Pacific Ocean and the predatory nature of a stowaway aboard his tiny lifeboat - a Bengal tiger with the improbable name of Richard Parker. The decade between the popular novel's publication and its adaptation on film was evidence of the story's inherent cinematic obstacles, foremost among them an ocean setting and a level of interaction between boy and tiger that no production would dare to risk, and no insurance company would dare to underwrite.iMaking Life of Pi was a very daunting task,i noted Twentieth Century Fox visual effects consultant David Conley who - along with visual effects producer Susan MacLeod - was involved from the earliest 1 / 32 stages of the project's development. 'There were many questions. How would we do the

water? How would we work with live animals and kids? Could we intercut between live LIFE OF PI animals and CG animals?" The most important question of all - and the one director Ang Lee needed to have answered before he would commit to the project - was whether or not Richard Parker, his film's second lead, could be authentically realized as a computer animated character. We had to convince the audience that Richard Parker was a real tiger on that boat with Pi, and that Pi was in real danger," said Conley. "Ang was adamant about that. I don't think he would have done this movie if he had thought the tiger would wind up looking CG. The job of persuading Lee that an utterly photorealistic CG tiger was feasible fell to production visual effects supervisor Bill Westenhofer, who would take up the challenge of creating that tiger with his longtime associates at Rhythm & Hues. "A CGI tiger was really the only way you could make this movie," said Westenhofer. "You couldn't do an animatronic tiger, and you couldn't use a real tiger throughout. Even if you had a perfectly trained tiger and you could get the studio legal department and the insurance company to allow that tiger to interact with a kid, they were going to be trapped together on a small boat. There was no way that could happen. So we knew we were going to have to achieve a completely photorealistic tiger for this show, and that was our goal. It was a goal similar to others that Rhythm & Hues had aimed for previously, most notably with the lion Aslan in the first Narnia film. But that had been a fantasy film, and the talking, emoting Aslan had been a fantasy character. That would not be the case for Life of Pi's tiger. I told our artists: 'We've done a lot of animals at R&H, and we've always tried to 2 / 32 make them photoreal - but then they had to talk and sing. This is the first time we're

LIFE OF PI going to do a real animal. This tiger is a real tiger, not a fantasy tiger - and it's your chance to fool your colleagues.""
